title: Backups, phrases and output
goal: How the generator adds a joined (+) way into every word beside its primary, merges two words into one stroke, and writes the dictionary files out.

blocks.x: Backup composition: every + way into a word

After every primary is locked, a fixed-point pass builds `+`-joined entries for every word it can, from a placed stem, an ending, a prefix, or the word's own syllables. A rare word can keep a terse one-stroke primary ([[machete|PHEFPT]]) and still be typed from its sound ([[PHU/+SHE/+TAOE]]).

items: There are about 205,400 backups in the current build.
They are placed before the bonus short forms.
A phrase never takes a backup of more than one stroke.
No backup can change a primary.
A word may have several. When two words compose the same text in one round, the more frequent word wins.

blocks.x: Common to all directions

items: A placed word's **fastest outline**, plus its own plain reading when that is a longer form.
A `+*` ladder marker on the stem is dropped: no join has a mid-join star.
A join of three or more strokes whose last stroke fits on the one before (right-hand keys, all later in steno order) is also offered folded.
A word's "best" outline, used as a stem in later rounds, is picked by strokes, then keys, then ergonomics, then outline text; never by entry order.
Joins through an ending build on the stem's plain reading, never its brief. Stem: three letters or more; the join must pass the fragment check; a word in `-ly` never joins through `-y`.
Each round's compositions are collected on every core, up to five rounds.

blocks.x: The directions

head: Direction
Mechanic
rows: Placed stem's outline plus a reduced trailing syllable as one joined stroke (build + -ing).
Stem found by spelling plus a known two-stroke suffix (`-ism`, `-ary`, `-ical`, ...).
OR a leading consonant cluster into a placed stem's first stroke when the keys are disjoint. No stroke added; later strokes carried through untouched.
A family member's stem outline, whatever it is, plus the ending's standalone stroke: call + -ed is [[KAUL/+-D]], look + -s is [[HRAOBG/+-S]]. Covers endings that are not a syllable, which (a) cannot.

The word, one syllable per stroke, from each pronunciation: its folded outline; a reduced last syllable struck like a suffix ([[TAEU/+-BL]]); every vowel written ([[TAEU/+PWUL]]); both syllable splits ([[HREPL/+UPB]], [[HRE/+PHUPB]]); a fixed prefix folded or alone. A kept schwa is always `U`. Needs no other word; runs in round 0 only.
A prefix's stroke, then the placed stem's whole outline joined: [[UPB/+KHRAOER]] (unclear), [[TKE/+KOED]] (decode), [[TPHOPB/+STOP]] (nonstop). The word's sound must end in the stem's.
Two placed words back to back, when the spelling is the two words joined (myself = my + self).
Same, found by letters and a loose consonant check, for pairs CMUdict does not split cleanly: [[PHO/+WUPB]] (noone = no + one). See [syllables and folding](#/ref/syllables).

blocks.x: Direction (f) uses eighteen prefixes: un, dis, mis, re, pre, de, co, en, im, in, non, sub, trans, anti, inter, semi, over, under. See [prefixes](#/ref/prefixes).
Endings used by direction (d)

head: List
Endings
rows: Family endings (also shape a family's primary)
Extra backup-only endings (never move a primary)
`-ation -ist -ish -ism -ize -ous -ive -ic -al -age -ity -ward -en -y -or -ible`, e.g. art + -ist is [[ART/+EUFT]] and sail + -or is [[SAEUL/+-R]]
`-or` is written with `-er`'s stroke and `-ible` with `-able`'s

blocks.x: Longest ending first: information is inform + -ation, never a non-word + -on. An ending that replaces part of the stem (`-tion`, `-ic`, `-ity`) is reached by the sound-based directions (a), (e), not by a spelling-based family link.
How many joined ways in
Every word of two or more syllables has joined ways in, however terse its primary. See [every way to join a word](#/ref/ways-to-join).
Phrase-briefing: two words in one stroke

Two words whose primaries share no keys have an unclaimed union stroke. "of" is `-F`, "the" is `-T`; their OR is [[-FT]], which writes both. "of the" is the commonest bigram in the corpus (2,766,332,391 occurrences). This section is the build mechanism; the phrases are on [phrase-briefing](#/ref/phrases).

head: Step
Rule
rows: The 20,000 most frequent bigrams, ranked by raw bigram count (not a collocation score).
Disjoint-OR of the two words' primaries.

One side may be a multi-stroke word. The single-stroke side merges into the other's **first** stroke only, by the disjoint-OR rule of direction (b); the rest of the host is carried through untouched: a (`A`) + currency (`KURPB/+SEU`) is `KAURPB/+SEU`.
A bigram's lowercase "i" is looked up as the "I" entry on [[EU]] (the pronoun, not the letter). `EU` shares vowel keys with most verbs, so few "I" phrases qualify; "I would" is [[WOEU]].

blocks.x: Who gives up a stroke
A pair whose merged stroke a word already holds competes for it on count. Limits:

head: Limit
Value
rows: the 5,000 most frequent (a phrase may still take one of their short forms or alternates)
Pairs allowed to take a held stroke at all
only the 1,000 most frequent eligible pairs; a rarer pair is committed only into a free stroke

blocks.x: Under these limits 134 words carry a star because a phrase took their stroke, 15 of them in the top 5,000. The build has 5,720 phrase entries.
The phrasing grammar

The phrasing grammar writes a whole phrase in one stroke by rule: starter (who) on the left bank, auxiliary or tense on the vowels, star for not, verb on the right bank. Lessons: [the lessons](#/lesson/19-phrasing-grammar), [the phrasing strokes lesson](#/lesson/20-phrasing-strokes).
Output: writing the dictionary files
The generator keys every word lowercase. `write_json` applies one transform on output, `written()`: the pronoun "i", alone, leading a contraction, or either half of a phrase, is capitalized.

head: Stroke
Written as
rows: eye (the letter i is not given this stroke)

blocks.x: A full `!build` takes about 8 seconds. `score --check-readme` takes about 4.6 seconds; `--write-readme` rewrites stale README tables.
Checks that run on every build and test run

items: No two raw entries share an outline (`write_json` keys by outline text; a duplicate would silently lose an entry).
A word's cheapest outline does not depend on entry order.
The top 1,000 words are one stroke each, with no `/+*` ladder marker. Only american and lt, which have no one-stroke candidate at all, are exempt.
The solver matches brute force on 300 random over-subscribed graphs.
No word sits on a worse outline than one of its own unclaimed candidates; every word in the top 2,000 has an outline.
A reduced "-er" keeps its R, and a sound may only explain a key on a stroke it can actually be on (each pinned by a test).
